fields.meta_title: What Is the Lord’s Supper? The Meaning of Communion
fields.description: The Lord’s Supper is Christ’s gift to his church — a remembrance of his death, a communion with the living Christ, and a foretaste of the coming feast.
fields.body_html:
On the night before he died, Jesus gathered his disciples for a meal and gave his church a gift that has been treasured ever since: the Lord’s Supper. Christians call it by several names — Communion, the Lord’s Table, the Eucharist (from the Greek for “thanksgiving”), the breaking of bread — but all of them point to the same simple, profound act. Taking bread and a cup of wine, Jesus said of the bread, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19), and of the cup, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). In these ordinary elements he gave his people an unforgettable way to remember, receive, and proclaim his saving death until he comes again.

What, then, is the Lord’s Supper, and why does it matter so much? Scripture gives it several rich layers of meaning, and each one deepens our love for the Saviour it points to.

It is a remembrance of Christ’s death

The first and clearest meaning is remembrance. “Do this in remembrance of me,” Jesus said — twice, according to Paul (1 Corinthians 11:24–25). The broken bread pictures his body given; the poured cup pictures his blood shed. At the table we are carried back to the cross and made to see again, with more than our eyes, the costly love that saved us. We do not merely think an idea; we taste and handle a sermon, preached in bread and wine.

There is a gentle wisdom in the fact that Christ gave us not only words to hear but a meal to taste. God made us with bodies and senses, and he meets us through them. The gospel is spoken in the sermon, but at the table it is placed in our hands and on our tongues, so that the truth reaches us by more doors than one. A doctrine can be argued with; a gift received into the hand is harder to hold at arm’s length. In the Supper, the love of God stops being merely an idea we consider and becomes something we handle, taste, and take in.

This is deeply intentional. We are forgetful people, and the good news is easy to let slip into the background of a busy life. So the Lord gave us a regular, physical, unmistakable reminder — a meal that stops us, gathers us, and says: look again at the cross; this is what your salvation cost; this is how loved you are. Every time we come, we “proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). The table is a living memorial that keeps the crucified Christ at the centre of his people’s life.

It is a real communion with Christ

Yet the Supper is more than a memory exercise. It is a genuine communion — a fellowship with the living Christ and a means by which he feeds our souls. Paul asks, “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). At the table, by faith, we do not merely recall an absent Saviour; we commune with a present one.

Jesus spoke of this nourishment in vivid terms: “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). Christians have understood this in different ways, but all agree on the heart of it: at the Lord’s Table the believer truly feeds on Christ by faith and is strengthened by him. The Supper is not empty ceremony; it is spiritual food. We come hungry and are fed; we come weak and are strengthened; we come cold and our love is rekindled at the memory of his.

It binds believers together as one body

Communion is never merely a private transaction between the soul and God; it is a family meal that knits the church together. Paul draws the line straight from the one loaf to the one people: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17). To share the table is to declare that we belong to one another because we belong to Christ.

This has always given the Lord’s Supper a reconciling power. It is hard to hold a grudge against a brother or sister with whom you are about to share the bread of Christ’s broken body. The table calls us to come in love and peace, and it exposes and heals the divisions we would rather ignore. Across every barrier of race, class, age, and nation, the one loaf makes one people — a foretaste of the great gathering of the redeemed from every tribe and tongue.

How often, and in what spirit, should we come?

The New Testament does not lay down a rigid schedule, but it clearly assumes the Supper will be frequent. The early believers “broke bread in their homes” regularly, receiving their food “with glad and generous hearts” (Acts 2:46), and Paul speaks of “as often as” they eat the bread and drink the cup (1 Corinthians 11:26) — expecting it to be a recurring rhythm of church life, not a rare event. Christians differ on exactly how often to gather at the table, but all agree it is meant to be a settled, treasured habit, not an afterthought.

Just as important as how often is in what spirit we come. The elements are bread and wine, not magic; there is no power in the mere eating. The blessing comes to those who receive by faith, looking through the signs to the Saviour they signify. To come superstitiously, as though the ritual itself saved, is to miss the point; to come faithlessly, treating it as an empty formality, is to miss the blessing. But to come believing — feeding on Christ in the heart, by faith, with thanksgiving — is to be truly nourished. The old writers on Communion loved to dwell on this inward feeding, urging worshippers to bring an empty, hungry, adoring heart, and to look away from the bread to the Bread of Life himself.

It looks back to the Passover and forward to the feast

Jesus instituted the Supper during the Passover meal, and that setting is full of meaning. For centuries Israel had eaten the Passover lamb to remember their rescue from slavery in Egypt, when the blood of a lamb turned away death. Now Jesus, “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7), gave the old feast a new and greater meaning: the true Lamb of God had come, and his blood would rescue his people from a deeper bondage than Egypt’s.

And the table looks forward as well as back. Jesus told his disciples he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again “until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom” (Matthew 26:29). Every Communion is therefore a rehearsal for a coming celebration — “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9), when the whole family of God will sit down together at the table of the King. We eat now in hope, tasting a small piece of a feast that will one day fill eternity.

How to come to the table

Because the Supper is so holy, Paul urges that we come thoughtfully, not carelessly. “Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28). This self-examination is not meant to keep the unworthy away — for none of us is worthy in ourselves — but to keep us from coming flippantly, with unconfessed sin or a heart at war with a brother. We come as sinners who need grace, not as saints who have earned a reward. The examination is a clearing of the heart before a feast, not a locked door before a stranger.

So come honestly: confess your sin, make peace where you can, and then come gladly. The table is not for the perfect but for the pardoned, not for the strong but for the hungry. It is one of the sweetest gifts Christ ever gave his church — a place to remember his love, to feed on him afresh, to be knit to his people, and to lift our eyes to his return. Few things in the Christian life gather so much into so small a space: past, present, and future; the individual soul and the whole family of God; sorrow over sin and joy in salvation, all held together in a piece of bread and a cup of wine. Rightly received, it sends us away not proud but grateful, and not the same. Whenever you come, come looking to Christ, and you will not go away empty. He set this table himself, and he is himself the host, the feast, and the One who makes the humblest guest welcome.
